title: The ways of prayer, looking back
tomorrow: Paul lists the commandments, then folds the page. into what?

cards: After a big night, the real questions come in the car home. In Luke, one of the disciples watches Jesus pray, waits until he's finished, and asks: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.”
Not how to preach. Not how to heal. How to pray.
People still ask it, in parking lots and at kitchen tables, some with no faith background at all.

teach.b: Christians have answered that request in more than one voice. Here are some, side by side, none ranked.
Benedictine: a monastery bell calling the community to pray the Psalms together at set hours, with work in between; Benedict's Rule asks that prayer be short and pure.
Orthodox: a short line repeated with the breath, the Jesus Prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, echoing the tax collector in Luke: “God be merciful to me a sinner.”

teach.h: A SCENE, A SILENCE, A SHOUT.
teach.b: Ignatian, from Ignatius of Loyola: stepping into a Gospel scene in your imagination, and at day's end looking back for where God was present.
Quaker: a room of people sitting in silence, waiting, until someone is moved to speak, or no one is. Pentecostal: hands raised, praise out loud, drawing on the day the Spirit came in Acts.

And under all of them, Paul's words for anyone who doesn't know where to start: “for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.”
So what does this give someone this week, with a friend's question in the air? Permission.
A bell, a breath, a scene, a silence, a shout. The disciples asked to be taught, and the answer had many rooms.

how: Christians pray in different ways: some keep set hours with the Psalms, some repeat the Jesus Prayer, some review the day in the Ignatian way, some sit in Quaker silence, and some pray aloud with hands raised.

games.q: what does “the ways of prayer” mean?
o: a single correct posture for prayer in church
the prayers a priest says during a service
the different ways Christians pray, side by side

p: Psalms at set hours, work between
the Jesus Prayer, with the breath

s: Christians all pray the same way
set hours, a breath prayer, imagining a scene, silence, praise out loud.
the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray
Luke 11:1: Lord, teach us to pray.
in Quaker worship, someone always has to speak
they wait in silence until someone is moved to speak, or no one is.

games.q: your coworker says she can't pray because her mind won't stop racing. which way from today might she try first?
o: only long, formal prayers count, so she should practice those.
a short line with the breath, like the Jesus Prayer, repeated slowly.
wait until her mind is calm, then begin praying.
games.why: a racing mind is one reason some Christians love the Jesus Prayer: one short line, with the breath. and Paul adds: we know not what we should pray for as we ought.

practice: Try the Quaker way for the sit: eyes closed, hands still, waiting without filling the silence. If words come, let them be few; if none come, Paul says the Spirit prays with groanings which cannot be uttered.
If you don't pray, just sit in the quiet and notice what it's like to wait without hurrying.

wordCard.voice: The ways of prayer. Benedictine hours, the Jesus Prayer, Ignatian imagining, Quaker silence and Pentecostal praise: many rooms, one request.

orig.note: Greek: to pray. Luke 11:1 uses this verb: Lord, teach us to pray.

carryVoice: Keep this one: your way to pray, one of many rooms. That's the summit's twenty-fifth day.
